The exterior of this volume is a fine example of 19th-century bookbinding. The central panel is decorated with marbled paper in a "snail" or "comb" pattern—so named for the delicate, swirling loops created by the artisan floating ink on a liquid bath. The spine is bound in brown pebbled leather, which provided durability for a frequently consulted medical reference. 

While much of the gold-leaf lettering on the spine has worn away, the following fragments remain visible:

<margin>Various judgments <note>original Latin: "iudicia"</note> concerning my writings.</margin>
I know full well that various and many strange judgments <note>original Latin: "iudicia"</note> concerning these works <note>original Latin: "Operibus"</note> of mine that I have just mentioned have been passed here and there; but what is one to do? One must let people talk until their gray beards fade away. 

<margin>I have always judged it to be the mark of a distinguished and wise man to dismiss the slanders <note>original Latin: "calumnias"</note> of fools and the wicked with a great spirit.</margin>
But I also speak and say that everyone should judge it as he understands it, according to whether he is inclined <note>original: "affectioniret," meaning to have a specific disposition or emotional bias</note> toward my person or toward the teaching of my aforementioned writings. The fool judges foolishly; the ignorant, ignorantly; the worldly, purely worldly; the mocker, mockingly; the envious, grudgingly; the slanderer, slanderously; the scorner, scornfully; **every bird sings according to how its beak has grown.** <note>A German proverb meaning people speak according to their nature and capacity.</note> The world rewards in no other way. 

<margin>Though we cannot all compose poetry <note>original: "dichten"</note>, yet we all wish to judge <note>original: "richten"</note>.</margin>
<margin>But a mind conscious of what is right laughs at the lies of rumor <note>original Latin: "Sed, Conscia mens recti, famæ mendacia ridet"</note>.</margin>
Be that as it may, I know for certain on the other hand—and can also prove it (where necessary) with many letters—that good people who understand the Art <note>original: "Kunstuerstendige"; likely referring to the "Sons of Art" or those initiated into alchemical knowledge</note>...

# Confession of Heinrich Khunrath
<page-num>116</page-num>

### Chapter V. 173

<margin>68</margin>
Since things are so, how is it possible for you (you **Cadaverous Simpleton** <note>original: *Casdauerischer Lappist*; "Cadaverist" was Khunrath's derogatory term for those who sought the Stone in human remains, while "Lappist" comes from the German *Lappe*, meaning a fool or simpleton</note>)—once the deathly separation and parting of the aforementioned Three <note>Body, Soul, and Spirit</note> has occurred (which must happen if **Regeneration** <note>original: *Regeneratio*</note> is to be otherwise accomplished)—to catch all three of them, each one individually for yourself, to keep them, to **purify what must be purified** <note>original: *depuranda depuriren*</note>, to compose them proportionally according to Nature, and to reunite them with one another into a new, **glorified** <note>original: *glorificirt*</note>, blessed **Body** <note>original: *Corpus*</note>?

# Chapter IX #

<margin>

What? You say; do you wish to criticize my arts? High and great people <note>referring to the nobility and princes who sponsored alchemists</note> are well pleased by them! It is true, I admit it: but on the other hand, it is also true that high-ranking people have often been led astray by deceivers. Wise people also sometimes commit great folly. Great lords have been led around in the **nose-dance** <note>original: *Nasendanze*; a German idiom for being mocked, deceived, or led by the nose</note> before, and have even led the procession in it themselves. 8. 
Furnace with the small pipe.
</margin>
Someone once fashioned a small copper or iron pipe filled with gold <note>original symbol: ☉ (Sol)</note> inside the melting furnace. He positioned the crucible—which contained materials containing no gold <note>original symbol: ☉ (Sol)</note>—so that it rested directly under the pipe. When the fire was properly started, the gold was intended to melt and flow into the crucible, thereby being proclaimed as "made gold." However, the ruse was uncovered, and it was revealed what kind of fellow that gold-maker really was.

They might have a small hole at the bottom and be hollow inside, where gold has been hidden so that it might fall out into the melt.

<margin>11. Lead containing silver and gold.</margin>

<margin>12. Silvered brass.</margin>
A new performance is currently being practiced with silvered brass, as follows: the deceiver has genuine brass fetched and cuts it into small pieces; but then the rogue has good silver, colored to look like brass (which he can do masterfully), <margin>SCH-M, O, MO. <note>These abbreviations likely refer to specific alchemical ingredients or stages in the fraudulent process, such as "Schmelz" (melt) or specific minerals.</note></margin> already prepared and cut into the same small shapes on his person. He swaps one for the other, sticking the real brass into a trick pocket <note>original: *Schiebesack*; a hidden or sliding pouch used by magicians and frauds for sleight of hand</note>, and layers the silvered brass in the crucible with his sophisticated materials <note>original: *Sophistischen materijs*; in this context, "sophistical" refers to deceptive or fake substances intended to mislead the observer</note>. He sets it to be cemented <term>Cementation: a process of refining gold by surrounding it with powdered materials and heating it to remove impurities.</term> and to flow; then he performs the cupellation, and thus he has "made" silver out of brass.

# Printed at Magdeburg / by the heirs of Andreas Gene. <note>Andreas Gene (also spelled Gehne) was a prominent printer in Magdeburg. It was common in the 16th century for a printing house to continue operating under the title of the "heirs" after the master's death to maintain the firm's established reputation.</note>

->IN THE YEAR<- <note>Original Latin: "ANNO"</note>

->1598<- <note>Original Roman numerals: CIƆ. IƆ. XCIIIX. The symbols CIƆ and IƆ are archaic typographic forms for 1,000 and 500. While the final digits are rendered unusually, the date corresponds to 1598.</note>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut printer's mark or tailpiece featuring a grotesque mask at the center. The mask is surrounded by elaborate scrollwork, wings, and floral swags, with a small decorative pendant hanging at the base.</image-desc>

<summary>This is the book's colophon, identifying that the work was printed in the German city of Magdeburg by the printing house of Andreas Gene's heirs in 1598.</summary>
<keywords>Magdeburg, Andreas Gene, printing history, colophon, 16th century, Germany, typography</keywords>
